title: Ombangulu
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Wingless white ants pounded with salt and cooked inside leaves — the name means toughened or compacted together, which is exactly what happens to them.
longDesc: Ombangulu is pounded white ants cooked in leaves, and the Lugbara name means toughened or compacted together. It is made from egbere, the early-morning type that emerges between half past four and six. That precision is characteristic: the Lugbara sort their white ants by the hour they come out of the ground, and each type has a use. The related dish alanda, also called amboroko, is a cake made from the small white ants.
ingredients: White ants (onya, ona or una) — the egbere type, with wings removed
steps: Remove the wings from the white ants.
Wrap the pounded mixture in leaves.
Cook the parcels until set and compacted together.
chefTips: Egbere is the type used for ombangulu — the early-morning emergence, between half past four and six in the morning. That is the Lugbara distinction and it is a real one.
The name tells you the doneness cue: toughened, compacted together. It should hold as a mass rather than staying loose.
Wings off before pounding. They will not soften and they taste of paper.
Alanda, also called amboroko, is the ant cake made from the small white ants, and it is the same family of preparation.

The Lugbara clock for white ants is worth learning: ondreondre or andre emerge 7.30 to 8.30 in the evening, immediately after dusk; api or inia between 11 and midnight as the second round; egbere 4.30 to 6 in the morning; and otunyo means yesterday's white ants, fermented two days.

Other insects have their own times and methods too: akuruma are collected in the mornings with noise made from tins and jerrycans; ifu or ofu in the late afternoon, three to four, with children singing; ica last of all before dusk, six to seven. Ese are grasshoppers, migrating in April and November — which tracks the Ganda May and November nsenene seasons closely.
No quantities and no timings are documented. Nothing here is estimated to cover that.
commonMistakes: Cooking it over flames rather than embers.
Using the wrong emergence type, which the Lugbara would not do.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which describes ombangulu as pounded wingless onya with salt, cooked in leaves, gives the literal meaning of the name as toughened or compacted together, records its other name bofolo, and names egbere as the type used for it. Alanda, also called amboroko, is given there as an ant cake from small white ants.

The emergence clock is from the same article: ondreondre or andre at 7.30 to 8.30 PM immediately after dusk; api or inia at 11 PM to midnight as the second round; egbere at 4.30 to 6.00 AM; otunyo meaning yesterday's white ants, fermented two days. It also records akuruma collected in the mornings with noise made from tins and jerrycans, ifu or ofu in the late afternoon at 3 to 4 PM with children singing, ica gathered before dusk at 6 to 7 PM, ese grasshoppers migrating in April and November, ombi locusts of which some are poisonous or forbidden, ozi wood ants near anthills, and nyaka as the general term for caught insects.

That article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material on Lugbara culture, and gives no quantities anywhere. Its taxonomy is treated as a lead list rather than established fact.
healthBenefits: Termites are high in protein, fat, iron and zinc.
Cooked in leaves with no added oil.
culturalNote: Sorting an insect by the hour it emerges, and cooking each type differently, is the kind of knowledge that only exists where people have watched the same anthills for generations. Four named emergence windows in a single night is a more detailed observation than most published entomology bothers with.
